newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada province paves way for tobacco lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Canada province paves way for tobacco lawsuit.

text.p: British Columbia announced legislation on Monday paving the way for the province to become the first in Canada to sue tobacco companies to recoup medical costs for treating smokers.
But the province said that before filing a lawsuit, it was asking the tobacco industry to compensate it voluntarily for tobacco-related illness and smoking prevention programs.
Provincial officials also demanded that cigarette companies acknowledge publicly that tobacco is addictive and causes cancer and lung and heart disease.

Legal experts said the proposed legislation made British Columbia likely the first government outside the United States to pursue such action against tobacco manufacturers, similar to the approach taken by 37 U.S. states.
Some tobacco companies reacted swiftly and derisively to the province's move.
"It seems as if their announcement is nothing more than a thinly disguised tax grab by another name," said Mary Trudelle, spokeswoman for RJR MacDonald in Toronto.
Political analysts said the legislation was aimed at forcing tobacco companies into negotiations over paying the costs of health care for smoking-related illness.

"I believe our readiness to take this action will force the industry to consider the other options we are presenting," British Columbia Health Minister Joy MacPhail said in a statement moments before a news conference to announce the measure.

She said the province was prepared to consider "other revenue measures such as licensing fees to ensure the industry pays its share of the cost of smoking prevention and the treatment of tobacco-related illnesses."
British Columbia's government-funded health care program pays out an estimated C$420 million to C$560 million (U.S.$311 million to $415 million) a year for smoking-related illnesses.
In the United States, negotiations were set to resume on Monday between state and federal government officials and cigarette makers over a multi-billion dollar settlement.
Canada's federal government said last month it was considering possible lawsuits against tobacco companies and other provinces were also said to be exploring the idea.
The incentives for governments to sue in Canada are even greater than in the United States because health care is provided universally and funded publicly.

But the risks are also greater. Damage awards have historically been far lower in Canada than in the United States, and under Canadian law, the government, if it lost, would be forced to pay the industry's legal costs.
Imperial Tobacco Ltd., a unit of Imasco Ltd. controls about 65 percent of the Canadian cigarette market. Imasco is 40 percent owned by B.A.T Industries Plc of Britain.

The second biggest company, Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc., is 60 percent owned by Rothmans Inc. and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos Inc.. Rothmans Inc is a unit of Rothmans International Plc, which is owned by Swiss luxury goods holding company Cie Financiere Richmont AG.
Third-ranked RJR MacDonald is wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International. American cigarette brands are also sold in Canada.
